newsitem.title: LEBANON: Disagreements delay new Lebanese government.
newsitem.headline: Disagreements delay new Lebanese government.

text.p: Lebanese leaders have run into disagreements on the composition of a new government and it is now not likely to be formed before next week, political sources said on Friday.

Most politicians originally expected Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri to complete the formation of the government by the middle of this week after a large majority of parliamentary deputies named him from the job.

However, a source close to the discussions said behind-the-scenes negotiations were stumbling over demands by President Elias Hrawi for a big say in the formation of the cabinet which Hariri was not ready to accept.
"The cabinet will not be formed until all the obstacles are removed. It is unlikely that it will be formed before next week," the source said.

Political sources said parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, the third member of Lebanon's ruling troika, was not involved in the current dispute between Hrawi and Berri but might make his own demands on the composition of the cabinet once they reached an agreement.
Newspapers said Hrawi wanted a cabinet with representatives of all major political forces and wanted to name four of the Christian ministers compared with only one in Hariri's outgoing government.
This would contrast with the homogeneity of the previous team, which included technocrats Hariri hand-picked and few ministers who questioned his policies.

Such a cabinet was likely to suffer public policy disagreements between its members, which Hariri has said he will not accept. He says the new cabinet must be harmonious and he will not tolerate any opposition within it.
The sources said Hariri wanted to bring back his supporters in the present cabinet and most of the 29 outgoing ministers, but Hrawi was refusing to accept some of them.
Hariri, who was reappointed for a third term on October 24 after parliamentary elections, has no time limit under the constitution for forming the government.
Newspapers said he was eager to form a cabinet but was prepared to wait until he got what he wanted.

"He will remain as prime minister-designate and caretaker prime minister until local and regional forces are fed up with the waiting game and offer him a bigger share in the next government," a columnist in the Beirut daily Nida'a al-Watan wrote.
